title: A Fun Way To Walk Your Class Across Campus
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes how he teaches his class to walk across campus with near-total independence, and argues that the payoff of this seemingly mundane routine extends far beyond hallway order. He begins the routine on day one with explicit, detailed instruction on pace, spacing, and posture, stays close to correct it early on, then deliberately withdraws his presence as students prove they can handle it. Once the standard routine is mastered, he escalates the challenge with variations such as watching from hiding, giving misdirection via a drawn map, walking in a herd instead of a line, and a game-like 'ninja' version of sneaking across campus. His central claim is that investing effort in a routine most teachers treat as trivial builds purpose, agency, and pride that transfers directly to academic work and study habits. The piece argues that trust and gradually handed-over responsibility, not constant supervision, are what mature students.
points: Teach a routine in exacting physical detail first (spacing, pace, posture) before ever expecting independence from it.
Deliberately withdraw your visible presence over time so students feel ownership and pride in performing the routine unsupervised.
Once a routine is mastered, escalate it with novel variations (hidden observation, misdirection, group movement) to keep raising the maturity bar.
Compliments students receive from other adults while performing the routine well reinforce the behavior more than teacher praise alone.
Effort poured into a 'mundane' routine like walking in line transfers to bigger things, including students' work and study habits.
quotes: Typically, when I walk a class across campus I let them do so without my input.
It’s something I begin teaching on the first day of school and then slowly release to them as the days and weeks go by.
The way I expect them to walk is taught in detail—uniform spacing, fast pace, head up and proud.
But as they get better, I move further away and rarely say a word. Eventually, I send them on their way as I watch from a distance.
The reason I put effort into a mundane routine is because it transfers to everything they do, including most importantly their work and study habits.
My favorite, however, is to sneak across campus like highly trained ninjas. Tiptoeing, hiding, crouching, laying behind bushes, stuck to walls around corners.
It builds comradery. It’s great fun. It creates a classroom culture students love being part of and are thus intrinsically motivated to push their own limits and look out for one another.
